traveler: Homer (Homeros; called Melesigenes in the ancient Life)
title: The Seven Cities and the One Grave: Homer, the Life That Was Written for Him
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Wilusa, the name in the Hittite archive
stops.date_confidence: [R] Late Bronze Age, no year recoverable. The identification of Wilusa with Ilios and of Ahhiyawa with a Mycenaean Greek power is the majority scholarly reading, not a certainty, and the primary Hittite tablets were not fetched during research; this rests on the dossier's summary. The pin is Troy's own canonical coordinate: the tablets were archived at Hattusa, and no stop is staged there.
stops.campa: Four centuries before any Greek writes the name Ilios, clerks in a Hittite chancery are filing correspondence about a western vassal called Wilusa and about a troublesome sea power they call Ahhiyawa. Treaties are drawn, oaths are sworn, quarrels over the same coastal strip are recorded and shelved. The scribes have no interest in poetry, and no idea that a language they have never heard will be singing about this shoreline half a millennium on. What they leave is narrow: the place existed, and it was fought over. Then the file goes back on the shelf.
suggested_refs: The Hittite Ahhiyawa texts and the treaties naming Wilusa
sources: Homer dossier summary of Hittite textual evidence; primary tablets not independently fetched

stops.name: Troy (Ilion), the anger of Achilles
stops.date_confidence: [R] traditional. The sack is dated to 1184 BCE on the Eratosthenic reckoning already used for Odysseus's itinerary. Homer's own act of composition is placed by modern scholars anywhere from c. 800-750 BCE (Powell), c. 750 (Janko), to c. 660-650 (M. L. West), a spread that is itself the evidence that no date exists.
stops.campa: The poem does not tell the war. It tells fifty-one days in the tenth year of it, a quarrel between two Greeks over a captive woman, and one man's refusal to fight. Achilles sulks, Patroclus dies in his armour, Hector is dragged three times around the walls, and an old king comes at night to kiss the hands that killed his son. Aeneas fights here and is carried off alive by a god; Virgil will build Rome on that one rescue. The city Homer burns leaves no archive behind it. Nobody can say what year it fell, or whether its king was called Priam.
stops.quote: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans. Many a brave soul did it send hurrying down to Hades, and many a hero did it yield a prey to dogs and vultures, for so were the counsels of Jove fulfilled from the day on which the son of Atreus, king of men, and great Achilles, first fell out with one another.
stops.quote_source: Homer, Iliad I, trans. Samuel Butler, Project Gutenberg ebook #2199
suggested_refs: The annotated recension of the Iliad Aristotle prepared for Alexander, kept under his pillow beside a dagger (Plutarch; treat as attested tradition)
sources: Homer, Iliad I, trans. Samuel Butler, Project Gutenberg #2199

stops.name: Hisarlik, the burned layer under the mound
stops.date_confidence: [A] archaeological. Wikipedia, 'Troy VII' dates the layer 1300-1180 BC and its destruction to around 1180 BC, roughly contemporary with the Late Bronze Age collapse. The research pool elsewhere carried c. 1220 BCE for the same layer; that figure is contradicted by the article and is not followed. Nothing ties the burning to any named person.
stops.campa: Nine cities stand and burn on one mound above the Dardanelles, each raised on the rubble of the last. The seventh settlement, walled, crowded, stocked as though for siege, goes down in fire around 1180 BCE. Four hundred years later, singers who have never seen the place will give that fire a cause, a cast and a ten-year calendar. No tablet from the ruin names a king, a fleet or a woman carried off, and no excavator has found one since. What is actually there is a band of ash between two floors.
suggested_refs: The burned stratum of Troy VIIa at Hisarlik
Heinrich Schliemann's excavation at Hisarlik from 1870 and his announcement of 1873

stops.name: Cyme, the ward of Cleanax
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated. The Life of Homer attributed to Herodotus is pseudonymous and probably 3rd-4th century CE (Wikipedia, 'Life of Homer (Pseudo-Herodotus)'), roughly a millennium after any plausible historical Homer. The year shown orders the segment and is not a claim: the source supplies no date whatever.
stops.campa: Critheis is a ward of Cleanax of Argos, a girl living in another man's house at Cyme in Aeolis, and she is pregnant by a man the story does not name. Her guardian weighs the household's standing against hers and sends her out of the city to Smyrna, where the swelling will not be watched. The Life that reports all this was written by an author pretending to be Herodotus, perhaps a thousand years after the fact, and it opens the poet's biography with a woman moved quietly out of town. It gives no date for any of it. It never names the father.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer (Vita Herodotea), sections 2-3

stops.name: Smyrna, born beside the Meles
stops.date_confidence: [R] for the birth, which is legendary and undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 3-4). [A] for the Homereum shrine on the Meles and for Homer's head on Smyrna's civic coinage, both historically attested (Wikipedia, 'Smyrna'). The year orders the segment.
stops.campa: The women of Smyrna keep a festival by the river, and Critheis, among them, gives birth on the bank. The child can see. She names him Melesigenes, born of the Meles, after the water she happened to be standing beside. Smyrna will raise a shrine on that bank, the Homereum, and strike his head onto its silver, and argue his birth against six other cities for the next thousand years. In the story as it stands here, at the water's edge, the name Homer has not been spoken yet.
suggested_refs: The Homereum on the banks of the Meles at Smyrna; Smyrnaean coinage bearing Homer's head

stops.name: Smyrna, the school of Phemius
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 4-8). The name Phemius is also that of the singer in the hall at Ithaca in Odyssey I, which is a standing reason to read this episode as back-formed from the poems rather than remembered independently.
stops.campa: Phemius keeps a school of letters and music in Smyrna. He takes in the woman who spins wool for him, marries her, adopts her son, and teaches the boy his own trade; when he dies he leaves him the school, the house and the pupils. The boy teaches from his stepfather's chair and is thought remarkable. The Life furnishes its poet a father and does not pause over where the name came from. A singer called Phemius also performs in the hall at Ithaca in the first book of the Odyssey, under duress, for the suitors.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 4-8

stops.name: Smyrna, the cave at the head of the river
stops.date_confidence: [R] later antiquarian tradition, undated (Wikipedia, 'Smyrna'). The cave's location is lost; the pin is the general Meles valley, not the cave.
stops.campa: Where the Meles rises there is a cave, and visitors are shown it as the room where the poems were made. Nobody in antiquity claims to have watched him work in it. The cave is simply pointed at, generation after generation, by people who need the composing to have happened somewhere a person can stand. What the tradition preserves is the demand behind the pointing, that a poem this size must have had an address. The hollow itself is lost now. Who first pointed at it, and on whose authority, no source says.
suggested_refs: The cave near the source of the Meles, shown in antiquity as Homer's composing place

segments.name: The Voyage of Mentes and the Losing of Sight

stops.name: Cumae, the voyage west into Tyrrhenia
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated legendary travel narrative (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 9). The source names 'Tyrrhenia' with no city; Cumae, the earliest Greek settlement toward Italy, is the researcher's placeholder pin for a claim that specifies no site at all. Mentes is also the disguise Athena takes in Odyssey I. Strabo's defense of Homer's geography at Geography 1.1.10 is attested and was verified on LacusCurtius.
stops.campa: Mentes of Leucas, who owns a ship and reads, comes into Smyrna, hears the young schoolmaster, and offers to pay his way if he will come and see the world. He shuts the school and goes. The itinerary the Life gives is a list of regions and not of harbours: Tyrrhenia, Iberia, the far west, named the way a man names places he has only been told about. Strabo will open his whole Geography arguing against Eratosthenes that this vagueness is deliberate craft, and that poetry is a kind of elementary philosophy.
stops.quote: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home.
stops.quote_source: Homer, Odyssey I, trans. Samuel Butler, Project Gutenberg ebook #1727
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 1.1.10, the defense of Homer against Eratosthenes (LacusCurtius, Loeb)

stops.name: Gadir, the far end of the itinerary
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated legendary travel narrative (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 9). 'Iberia' is named with no city or landmark; the Phoenician town of Gadir is the researcher's placeholder pin at the westernmost point Greek tradition attached to the word, not a site the source specifies.
stops.campa: Iberia, says the Life, and stops there. No city, no landfall, no river mouth, no name of a man who housed him. The Phoenician town at the ocean's edge is the westernmost thing Greek tradition ever attached to that word, so the voyage is pinned here for want of anything the source is willing to name. Whether he saw the Atlantic, or whether a later biographer simply needed the geography in the poems to have been earned somewhere, the text gives no way to decide.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 9, the westward voyage with Mentes

stops.name: Ithaca, the eyes begin to fail
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 10). This Ithacan version of the onset of blindness contradicts the Colophon version recorded in the same Life, which its own biographer prefers; both are carried here and neither is resolved. The pin is the canonical Ithaca coordinate used for Odysseus's homecoming.
stops.campa: On the island the ship puts in at, his eyes sicken. Mentes has business elsewhere and leaves him with Mentor, son of Alcimus, who nurses him and tells him the local stories: the king who sailed to Troy and took twenty years coming home, the wife at the loom, the old dog on the dung heap, the orchard. Ithaca claims ever after that the blindness began here. In this telling, Odysseus is something he is told about while lying sick in a borrowed bed, by a man named Mentor, which is also the name Athena borrows in the Odyssey when she wants the shape of a trustworthy older man.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 10

stops.name: Colophon, the light goes out
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 15); directly contradicts the Ithacan tradition in the same text. Xenophanes (c. 570 - c. 478 BCE) was born at Colophon and left it around 545 BCE, spending his life in Sicily and Magna Graecia; his fragment is undated within that long life and is not pinned to Colophon here. The quoted wording is Burnet's translation of DK 21 B11 as preserved by Sextus Empiricus.
stops.campa: The disease comes back at Colophon and finishes its work, and the biographer, who has just reported the Ithacan claim, says plainly that this is where the sight went. The two accounts cannot both stand, and the Life carries them both without choosing. Colophon also enters the list of cities claiming his birth, so one town ends up holding two incompatible pieces of him. Two centuries on, a Colophonian named Xenophanes leaves the town for the west and spends a long life attacking the gods this blind man handed the Greeks.
stops.quote: Homer and Hesiod have ascribed to the gods all things that are a shame and a disgrace among mortals, stealings and adulteries and deceivings of one another.
stops.quote_source: Xenophanes of Colophon, fragment DK 21 B11, preserved by Sextus Empiricus; trans. John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy
suggested_refs: Sextus Empiricus, Adversus Mathematicos, where the Xenophanes fragment survives
sources: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy, 'Fragments of Xenophanes', fr. 11

stops.name: Larissa Phriconis, the road back up the coast
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 15-16). Coordinates corrected during verification to the conventional site, a hilltop beside Buruncuk near Menemen overlooking the Gediz, per Wikipedia, 'Larissa (Aeolis)'; the earlier pin in the research pool was about 14 km off. The identification of that hill with the Larissa of the text is itself disputed among archaeologists.
stops.campa: Blind now, he turns back up the coast toward Cyme by way of Larissa, an Aeolian hill town above the Hermos. He has no school now, no property, no sighted companion and no destination past the next town; from here on he travels on other people's charity. Modern topographers are not agreed that the hill beside Buruncuk is even the Larissa meant, so the one hard noun in the sentence is unsteady too. The Life gives the place a single line: a name on a road, and nothing else.
suggested_refs: The hilltop site beside Buruncuk, conventionally identified with Larissa Phriconis

stops.name: Neonteichos, the leatherworker's poplar
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 16). Neonteichos is not securely located by modern topography; ancient testimony places it roughly thirty stadia from Larisa on the Hermus, and this pin is a point inside that band rather than a verified site. The research pool's earlier coordinate inherited the mistaken Larissa pin and has been moved.
stops.campa: At Neonteichos he sits down by the bench of Tychius, a leatherworker, and sings for his supper: the seven against Thebes, the expedition of Amphiaraus, hymns to the gods. Tychius feeds him and lets him sleep in the shop. A poplar stood where he performed, and men were still pointing at that tree centuries later, which is the usual way this tradition keeps a thing: not the poem, not the man, but the spot. The town itself has since gone missing, fixed by no excavator. The song of Amphiaraus is lost entire.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 16, the poplar at Neonteichos

stops.name: Cyme, the council and the word homeros
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 16); no record of any such council proceeding survives. The derivation of the name from homeros is a folk etymology, and the ordinary Greek sense of the word, hostage or pledge, supplies a rival explanation that no source adjudicates. Lucian's True History, quoted here, is second-century CE satire and declares itself fiction.
stops.campa: He comes back to the city his mother was sent away from and asks its council to keep him at public expense; in exchange, he says, he will make Cyme famous. A councillor rises to observe that if the city undertakes to feed every homeros who asks, it will be feeding a crowd. The word means a blind man in the local usage and a hostage or a pledge in ordinary Greek, and it is the only name anybody has called him since. The petition fails. He walks out cursing the place with obscurity.
stops.quote: he said indeed he was a Babylonian, and among his own countrymen not called Homer but Tigranes
stops.quote_source: Lucian of Samosata, True History II, trans. Francis Hickes, Project Gutenberg ebook #45858
suggested_refs: Lucian, True History II, the interview with Homer in the afterlife
sources: Lucian, True History II, trans. Francis Hickes, Project Gutenberg #45858

segments.name: Phocaea to Chios: the Poems in Another Man's Hand

stops.name: Phocaea, the poems taken down
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 17). No historical Thestorides is attested anywhere outside the biographical tradition. Coordinates from Wikipedia, 'Phocaea'.
stops.campa: Thestorides keeps a school at Phocaea and makes an offer: food, a roof, and in return the right to write down whatever the blind man already has by heart and whatever he composes next. It is the first transaction in the whole tradition where the poems become objects, detachable from the mouth that makes them. Nothing outside this story shows that such a man ever lived, which does not make the story about him any less precise. Thestorides copies, thanks him, sails for Chios, and performs the poems there under his own name.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 17, the bargain with Thestorides

stops.name: Erythrae, asking for the crossing
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 18). Coordinates from Wikipedia, 'Erythrae'.
stops.campa: Word comes back over the water that a schoolmaster on Chios is winning a reputation with poems that are supposedly his own. He walks down to Erythrae on the headland facing the island, a strait narrow enough to see across on a clear day, and asks fishermen for passage. They are going out anyway. The Life says nothing about what he paid them, or how long the crossing took. No confrontation is ever staged at the far end of this crossing: Thestorides hears he is coming and leaves the island before the boat lands.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 18

stops.name: Pithys, the dogs and the goatherd
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 19-20). Ancient Pithys is not independently located; the pin is the Volissos area it is conventionally associated with, corrected during verification to Wikipedia's coordinates for Volissos, 38.483 / 25.975. The research pool's earlier pin fell about 5.4 km west, in the sea.
stops.campa: He lands on the wrong side of the island and walks inland at Pithys, where a farm's dogs come at him in the dark. A goatherd called Glaucus hears the noise, calls them off, and takes the blind stranger back to his hut with bread and goat's cheese, then sits up half the night asking him questions. In the morning Glaucus walks him over to his employer, having decided on his own account that this is not an ordinary beggar. The employer is a man of property near Bolissus.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 19-20, Glaucus the goatherd

stops.name: Bolissus, tutor in the house above the sea
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 20-21). Coordinates corrected to Wikipedia's for Volissos. The marble plate at the village entrance quotes 'Herodotus' on Homer's residence there, but the sentence is from the pseudonymous Life and not from Herodotus; the confusion is live and is noted rather than repeated.
stops.campa: The landowner hires him to teach his children, and for the first time since Phocaea he is fed for his mind rather than his misfortune. Volissos still shows a marble plate at the village entrance quoting Herodotus on the poet who lived here, though the sentence is not Herodotus and never was. Here, says the Life, he makes the light poems: the Cercopes, the battle of the frogs and the mice, the small comic pieces that later ages could never decide whether to let him keep.
suggested_refs: The marble plate at the entrance to Volissos, Chios

stops.name: Chios town, the school and the two daughters
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 21-23); this is the only ancient Life to give Homer a developed domestic ending. Coordinates corrected during verification to Wikipedia, 'Chios (town)', 38.3725 / 26.1375; the research pool's earlier figure was the island centroid, some 7 km inland.
stops.campa: He moves down into the town, opens a school of his own, and teaches poetry as a discipline with rules that can be stated. It works. He grows prosperous, marries, fathers two daughters. One dies unmarried. The other is married to a Chian, and a separate legend has her dowry include an entire epic, the Cypria, handed over to Stasinus of Cyprus, which was antiquity's way of explaining why that poem circulated under two names. Neither daughter is named in the text that reports them.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 21-23
Ancient testimonia on the disputed authorship of the Cypria

stops.name: Daskalopetra, the seat cut in the rock
stops.date_confidence: [R] local tradition with no ancient textual confirmation that this rock is the referent (Wikipedia, 'Chios'). Archaeologists read the monument as a sanctuary, commonly of Cybele. Coordinates reconciled during verification to 38.4136 / 26.1394 at Vrontados; the geography and afterlife lenses of the research pool disagreed by about 2 km.
stops.campa: Above the shore at Vrontados a block of rock carries a cut seat and the remains of a shrine, and Chios has shown it for centuries as the place where he sat and taught. Archaeologists read the stone as a sanctuary of Cybele. The rock is real and the cutting is ancient, and nothing on it says who sat there. The district around it is called Omiroupoli, Homer's city; the island's airport carries his name; Vrontados claims his birth as well, against Smyrna.
suggested_refs: Daskalopetra, the rock-cut monument at Vrontados, Chios

segments.name: The Oracle, the Contest, and the Nile

stops.name: Delphi, the enigma of the young children
stops.date_confidence: [R] legendary, reported by Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.24.2, in the second century CE. Perseus and LacusCurtius could not be rendered for that section during research, so the oracle's exact wording is unverified. A 'Tomb of Homer' Wikipedia article cited in the research pool for this item does not exist and has been dropped. The year shown orders the segment.
stops.campa: He climbs to Apollo's oracle and asks the god the question every biography of him asks: who his parents were, and where he came from. What he is given is not an answer. He is told to beware the enigma of the young children, and sent away. Pausanias records the response centuries later, by which time everyone reading it knows how the death goes and can hear the warning as a prophecy. On the matter of the parents, the god is not reported as having said anything at all.
suggested_refs: Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.24.2
The silver bowl said in the Contest tradition to have been dedicated by Homer to Apollo at Delphi
sources: Pausanias 10.24.2, reported at second hand; primary text not retrievable during research

stops.name: Chalcis, the contest at the funeral games
stops.date_confidence: [R] The Certamen of Homer and Hesiod is a second-century CE text, naming Hadrian at line 33 and possibly deriving from Alcidamas' fourth-century BCE Mouseion (Wikipedia, 'Contest of Homer and Hesiod'). Hesiod, Works and Days 650-662, describes the voyage from Aulis, the games and the tripod, but does not mention Homer. Hesiod supplies no date; the year shown orders the segment. Most modern dating makes the two poets non-contemporaries.
stops.campa: Amphidamas of Chalcis dies and his sons hold games. Hesiod crosses from Aulis, the only sea voyage he ever admits to making, competes, wins a bronze tripod, and carries it up Helicon to dedicate to the Muses who taught him. Everything else arrives later and keeps growing for the better part of a thousand years: the contest between the two greatest poets alive, the riddles traded back and forth, the judge who prefers the man who sings of farming to the man who sings of war. Hesiod's own account of that day names no rival.
stops.quote: Homer and Hesiod were the first to compose Theogonies, and give the gods their epithets, to allot them their several offices and occupations, and describe their forms; and they lived but four hundred years before my time, as I believe.
suggested_refs: Hesiod, Works and Days 650-662
The Certamen Homeri et Hesiodi

stops.name: Thebes in Egypt, the priests' claim
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the passage, verified verbatim on LacusCurtius: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 1.96.2, first century BCE. [R] for its content, which is a priestly claim of cultural priority and a recurring pattern in Diodorus's first book. The passage names no Egyptian city; Karnak at Thebes is the researcher's placeholder pin, as with Tyrrhenia and Iberia above. The year shown orders the segment.
stops.campa: The priests of Egyptian Thebes told Greek visitors, and went on telling them for centuries, that the whole Greek stock of wisdom had been carried home from here. Their list of debtors is long and specific: Orpheus, Musaeus, Melampus, Daedalus, Homer, Lycurgus of Sparta, Solon, Plato, Pythagoras, Eudoxus, Democritus of Abdera. Diodorus writes it down without comment. No temple, teacher, or city is named on the Greek side of the claim, and no Greek source anywhere records the visit.
suggested_refs: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 1.96.2 (LacusCurtius)
sources: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 1.96.2, verified on LacusCurtius

stops.name: Samos, taken in at the Apaturia
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 26). The year and month shown order the segment.
stops.campa: Sailing for Athens, he is put ashore on Samos for the winter. The Apaturia is running, the festival at which the phratries enroll their sons and confirm on oath who belongs to whom. A phratry takes the stranger in, feeds him through the ceremony, and keeps him through the cold months while he sings for them. He has no city, no phratry, and no father's name anyone will vouch for, which is the whole of what the festival exists to establish. The oath-taking goes on around him.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 26

stops.name: Samos, driven from the sacrifice
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 26). The month shown separates this stop from the preceding one and carries no evidential weight.
stops.campa: A priestess is sacrificing to Kourotrophos, the goddess who rears the young, and she orders him away from the rite. He answers her with a curse. The exchange is preserved afterward as a point of ritual etiquette: who may stand at which sacrifice, and what a beggar at the edge of one is owed. The Life reports the insult and the reply at equal length and does not say which of them was in the right, nor whether the curse was thought to have taken. Nothing in the account explains why she refused him.
stops.quote: See now, how men lay blame upon us gods for what is after all nothing but their own folly.
stops.quote_source: Homer, Odyssey I, speech of Zeus, trans. Samuel Butler, Project Gutenberg ebook #1727
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 26

stops.name: Samos, the potters and the Eiresione
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 32-34). The midwinter dating of the Eiresione follows the episode's own description of the season, not a source's date.
stops.campa: The potters call him over to the kiln and offer to pay for a song while the pots are firing. He gives them the Kiln: Athena's hand laid on the work if they pay him what they said, and if they cheat him, cracked ware, black smoke, and demons loose in the furnace. Through the same midwinter he goes from door to door with the sons of the well-off houses singing the Eiresione, the beggar's blessing on a household, in exchange for whatever the door hands out.
suggested_refs: The Kiln (Kaminos) and the Eiresione, minor poems attributed to Homer in the Life

stops.name: Ios, put ashore sick
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 35-36). Coordinates approximate: the pin is the northern-coast area at Plaketos that nineteenth-century travelers were shown as the landing and tomb ground. The year and month order the segment.
stops.campa: The crossing toward Athens goes wrong. He is ill by the time the ship reaches Ios, cannot go on, and is set down on the northern shore at a place the islanders call Plaketos. The Life dates nothing here and names no month and no year. It does not say who was aboard with him, or who paid his passage. The biographer is careful on one point and repeats it: the illness comes first, before any riddle, and the illness is what kills him. He stays on that stretch of beach for days.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 35-36

stops.name: Ios, the riddle of the fishermen's boys
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated (Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 35-36). The two versions of the cause of death contradict each other inside the ancient tradition itself: Pseudo-Herodotus reports the riddle and explicitly rejects it as the cause, while other Lives make the failure to solve it exactly that. No source adjudicates and neither is resolved here.
stops.campa: One line of the tradition has him fail a riddle put to him on the beach, take the failure hard, and die of it; the biographer who records the riddle rejects that ending flatly and keeps the fever. Both versions are ancient, both were in circulation at once, and nothing survives from either side that stands between them. Boys come up from the water and he asks them what they have caught. What we caught we left behind, they tell him, and what we could not catch we carry. They mean lice.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Herodotus, Life of Homer sec. 35-36; the competing riddle-death tradition in the other ancient Lives

stops.name: Ios, buried above the shore
stops.date_confidence: [R] legendary. The burial is undated and unverifiable; the epigrams of Alcaeus of Messene in the Greek Anthology, c. 2nd century BCE, are the earliest literary tradition fixing the death-place on Ios (Wikipedia, 'Homer'). Two candidate sites, Plaketos and Agia Theodoti, are reported on the island and they conflict.
stops.campa: His companions and the islanders bury him near the sea and cut an epitaph over him calling the head beneath the earth divine. Alcaeus of Messene will write two epigrams congratulating the small island on what it holds. The grave is the one fixed point in a biography otherwise made entirely of rival claims. Six or seven cities want his birth, and in a thousand years of quarrelling over the rest of him nobody has contested the burial. Only Ios wants his death.
stops.quote: Men come and go as leaves year by year upon the trees. Those of autumn the wind sheds upon the ground, but when spring returns the forest buds forth with fresh vines. Even so is it with the generations of mankind, the new spring up as the old are passing away.
stops.quote_source: Homer, Iliad VI, Glaucus to Diomede, trans. Samuel Butler
suggested_refs: The epigrams of Alcaeus of Messene on Homer's tomb, Greek Anthology

stops.name: Ios, the grave dug for
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the searches, which are attested and dated: Pasch van Krienen's expedition with Spyridon Valetas in 1771, and Theodore and Mabel Bent's visit on 25 January 1884, a three-hour ride to Plaketos to see the tomb of the poet who 'died here on his way from Samos to Athens' (Wikipedia, 'Ios (island)'). [R] for any connection between the site and Homer. The stop is posthumous by some twenty-five centuries and is flagged for the operator in the report.
stops.campa: The grave is looked for, and in 1771 it is found: a stone near the chapel of Agia Aikaterini, inscribed to say that here under the earth lies the sacred head of heroic Homer. Then the man who found it reads the Greek a second time, sees that the grammar is wrong, and publishes his own doubt. The island offers a second candidate site at Agia Theodoti. By 1884 the Plaketos tomb is a standard three-hour excursion, and a bust of him now stands at the port of Gialos.
suggested_refs: The tomb site at Plaketos and the rival candidate at Agia Theodoti, Ios
The modern bust of Homer at the port of Gialos

stops.name: Salamis in Cyprus, an epic given away with a daughter
stops.date_confidence: [R] legendary transmission narrative, undated; transmitted in the Homeric biographical tradition and summarized in the Proclus Chrestomathy material. No primary text was fetched during research. The daughter is unnamed in every version. The year shown orders the segment.
stops.campa: The Cypria tells everything the Iliad leaves out: the wedding of Peleus, the apple, the judgment, the mustering of the ships, the nine years before the great poem opens. Antiquity could not agree who made it. One account had it reach Stasinus of Cyprus as the dowry of Homer's unnamed daughter, which turns an epic into a possession that can be signed over along with a girl. Another said Stasinus wrote it himself and traded on the name he had married into. The daughter goes unnamed in every version.
suggested_refs: Ancient testimonia on the authorship of the Cypria
sources: Homer biographical tradition, summarized in the Proclus Chrestomathy material; primary text not fetched

stops.name: Argos, a city that claims him
stops.date_confidence: [R] competing birthplace claim, undated. Hero-cult honors for Homer are reported at Argos alongside Smyrna, Chios and Ios in Hellenistic-era testimony, not independently refetched during research. Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae 3.11, surveys the birthplace dispute; the passage was not fetched. The year shown orders the segment.
stops.campa: Argos puts in its claim and backs it with cult, offering sacrifice to him as a hero, in a city with no Ionian coastline and no Aeolic in its speech. The claimant list runs to seven names in most ancient versions and to more in some, and the seven are not the same seven from one author to the next. Argos's own case rests on the hero-cult and on nothing else at all. Aulus Gellius, writing in Rome, surveys the whole quarrel at length and declines to settle it.
suggested_refs: Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae 3.11, on the dispute over Homer's birthplace
sources: Homer dossier summary of Hellenistic hero-cult testimony; primary sources not refetched

stops.name: Salamis, the island's claim
stops.date_confidence: [R] competing birthplace claim, undated, named as tradition only in the ancient 'Seven Cities' survey; not independently confirmed against a fetched primary text during research. The year shown orders the segment.
stops.campa: Salamis in the Saronic Gulf appears on the standard list of claimants, and nothing survives to say on what ground. The lists are the datum rather than the evidence. By the classical period the cities are competing for him the way they compete for a founding hero or the site of a temple, with the same machinery of local testimony and civic pride. What the competition establishes is that by then he was worth claiming. On the Salaminian side there is no shrine, no family, no named local historian: only the place on the list.
suggested_refs: The ancient 'Seven Cities' birthplace epigram and its variant lists
sources: Ancient 'Seven Cities' tradition as surveyed in classical testimony; not independently fetched

stops.name: Rhodes, the seventh name
stops.date_confidence: [R] competing birthplace claim, undated, named as tradition only; not independently confirmed against a fetched primary text during research. The year shown orders the segment.
stops.campa: Rhodes closes most versions of the seven-cities list. The verse that counts the contenders survives in several forms and the names shift between them, so the number seven stays fixed while its contents do not. Colophon, which the same tradition makes the place he went blind, sits on the list as a birthplace too, so at least one town is holding two claims at once. For Rhodes there is no document, no shrine, no family and no local historian cited anywhere.
suggested_refs: The variant recensions of the seven-cities epigram
sources: Ancient 'Seven Cities' tradition as surveyed in classical testimony; not independently fetched

stops.name: Pylos, the grandson of Nestor
stops.date_confidence: [R] late legendary genealogy, transmitted in the Hadrianic-era oracle tradition of the second century CE; no primary text was fetched during research. The year shown orders the segment and is emphatically not a date. Coordinates corrected during verification to the Palace of Nestor at Epano Englianos (Wikipedia, 'Palace of Nestor'); the research pool's earlier pin was about 900 m off.
stops.campa: The last genealogy that the ancient world built for him made him a great-grandson of Neleus: son of Telemachus and of Polycaste, Nestor's daughter, married into the house whose old king talks longest in the Iliad. It sets the poet inside the family of his own characters, one generation after the war he describes, and it is the only version of his life in which he has a father at all. An oracle delivered in the reign of Hadrian is where it comes from.
suggested_refs: The Palace of Nestor at Epano Englianos
The Hadrianic Delphic oracle on Homer's descent
